cards.explanation: The answer is True. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, was angry with his chief cupbearer and chief baker, and he put them in the captain of the guard's house, “…the same prison where Joseph was confined.” (Genesis 40:3) Joseph didn't have to go looking for company, friends. Two of the king's own officers got delivered right to him.

The answer is Joseph. The captain of the guard assigned the two officers to him, and verse 4 says he became their personal attendant (Genesis 40:4). So a man held in that prison is now looking after two of Pharaoh's officers. I think that's a strange spot to be in, and he does it anyway.

The answer is distraught, friends. Verse 6 says that's what Joseph saw when he came to them in the morning (Genesis 40:6). That's more than a rough night's sleep. Whatever those dreams were, they left these two in a heavy place.

The trouble is that no one can interpret the dreams, friends. The cupbearer and the baker tell Joseph, “We both had dreams…” and then, “but there is no one to interpret them.” (Genesis 40:8) They have the dreams in hand already. What they don't have is anyone to tell them what the dreams mean.

The answer is God. Joseph asks, “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” and then tells the men, “Tell me your dreams.” (Genesis 40:8) Notice where he points, friends. He doesn't put himself at the center of the room. He points up.

The cupbearer squeezes the grapes into the cup for Pharaoh. He says in his dream, “…I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand.” (Genesis 40:11) Fresh-squeezed service, straight to the king. The cupbearer was doing the job he knew.

The answer is that Pharaoh will restore him to his position. Joseph says, “Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position.” (Genesis 40:13) Then he adds that the cupbearer will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, just as he did before. Good news, friends, and it comes with a clock of three days.

The answer is False, friends. Joseph tells the cupbearer, “…even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon.” (Genesis 40:15) He says it right after telling how he was kidnapped. He is asking to be remembered, and he is saying plainly that he doesn't belong there.

The answer is three. The chief baker says, “…three baskets of white bread on my head.” (Genesis 40:16) Three is also the number in the cupbearer's dream, where there were three branches. Joseph is about to tell the baker what those baskets mean.

Birds are eating the baked goods out of the basket. In the top basket are all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, “…but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.” (Genesis 40:17) Me, I'd be waving my mustache at those birds and hollering, friends. Those baked goods were meant for Pharaoh, and the birds are the ones eating them.

The answer is False, friends, and it's a heavy one. Joseph tells the baker, “Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree.” (Genesis 40:19) The cupbearer's dream pointed to being restored, and the baker's pointed the other way. I think this part of the story hurts.

The occasion is Pharaoh's birthday. Verse 20 says, “On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his officials…” That's the same three days Joseph had named for both men. A feast for all those officials? My oven timer gets nervous just thinking about it.

The answer is True, and it's a sober one. Verse 22 says, “But Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation.” (Genesis 40:22) The three days passed and what Joseph said came to pass. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.

The cupbearer forgets all about Joseph. The text says, “The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.” (Genesis 40:23) Joseph had asked him, “…please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh…” (Genesis 40:14) I think that stings, friends, because Joseph asked so plainly.
